title: Introduction; personal data; parents and family
description: Isabel Miller begins the interview at Mabelle Morris's home in Elk River and records personal information about her birth in Rockwood, Ontario in 1887, her name, and her arrival in Idaho in 1907. Morris gives details about her mother Euphemia Campbell, her father John Robert Nickell, a bridge construction man, and her four sisters. She also names her husband William George Morris and their two children, Lillian and John.

title: Education and work; Elk River's boom and decline
description: Morris describes her high school education, post office work, and lifelong work in the drugstore. She explains how Elk River grew to 1,200 people as a Potlatch company town that built and rented the houses, and how the town emptied when the mill closed, with houses moved to Moscow, Troy, and Deary.

title: Sewing; homemaking; clubs and community service
description: Morris tells how she learned to sew as a girl by cutting doll dresses from her mother's fabric and handkerchiefs, and made clothing all her life. She recalls gardening from four in the morning, working long store hours, and her service in the Eastern Star, Rebekahs, election boards, and wartime registration.

title: Childhood memories; move west; courtship
description: Morris reflects on preferring rural life and recalls her Ontario farm childhood with a creek-side milk house and visiting cousins. She explains how uncles in Duluth and Potlatch brought her west to the post office job, and how her future father-in-law matchmade her meeting with William Morris, whom she married in Spokane in 1909.

title: Cashier work; sisters; world travels
description: Morris describes cashier work at the Potlatch company store, with pneumatic tubes and expert mental addition. She tells of her unmarried dietician sisters' world travels and her own two cruises with them, visiting Japan, India, Australia, Africa, Hawaii, Easter Island, and the royal garden party in England.

title: Elk River changes; mill closure and fire; drugstore years
description: Morris discusses Elk River's decline after the big mill was moved to Lewiston and the old mill was burned at night, an event lit so brightly a plane circled the town. She recounts how she and her husband came to start the drugstore, bought out a competitor, worked long hours, and fished the local creeks for trout.

title: Old Elk River buildings; Japanese residents; hospital and church
description: Looking at photographs, Morris identifies the family drugstore and hardware building, the brick store they bought, and the former business street with its laundry, Japanese dentist and photographer, and picture show. She recalls the Japanese mill workers and their later reunion in Japan, the town hospital, and the Potlatch-donated church whose windows were broken during the Depression.

title: Church windows; Depression business; Deep Creek mining
description: Mabelle discusses stained glass windows in the local church and a man who wanted to buy them. The conversation shifts to the Depression's impact on local business and Mr. Morris's gold mining efforts at Deep Creek to stay occupied.

title: Childrearing support; working in store
description: Mabelle explains the availability of a local doctor and help from sisters-in-law when her children were born. She describes living behind the store and how both children worked there as they grew.

title: John's education and career
description: Mabelle recounts son John's path from high school graduation at 16, to Parkes Air College in St. Louis, to his decision during the Depression to become a druggist and his current long work hours.

title: Daughter's teaching career; marriage to Chuck
description: Mabelle describes her daughter's education at Moscow and Lewiston, her teaching career in Elk River, meeting her husband Chuck (a Potlatch personnel worker), and their current split time between Bovil and Arizona.

title: Weekly work schedule; social visiting
description: Mabelle outlines the strict weekly routine of washing, ironing, cleaning, and baking. She explains how they would finish work and then visit friends, play cards, and share meals.

title: Community clubs; babysitters; village life
description: Mabelle details beach clubs, potluck dinners, Sunday musical gatherings, and picnic outings. She emphasizes the community was not isolated and that undesirable workers were fired by the mill, keeping the town cohesive.

title: Husband's sudden death; widowhood
description: Mabelle recounts her husband's unexpected death from a heart attack while hunting. She discusses the shock, her lack of prior worry about widowhood, and how she returned to work immediately.

title: Widow's pensions; women's financial support
description: Mabelle explains how widows of lumber workers received insurance or pensions until remarriage. She notes there was no other insurance or support system available.

title: Red Cross work; Depression gardening
description: Mabelle describes her Red Cross volunteer work during World War I, organizing women and cutting materials. She explains how gardening, canning, and baking helped families during the Depression.

title: Modern women vs. traditional skills
description: Mabelle contrasts her own knowledge of canning and bread-making with younger women who rely on canned goods. She credits her mother with teaching her these skills before marriage.

title: Current media; morning volunteer work
description: Mabelle lists her magazine subscriptions (National Geographic, AARP, Arizona Highways, Sunset) and television preferences. She describes her current routine of helping cook meals in the mornings.

title: Store decision-making; domestic help
description: Mabelle discusses working alongside her husband in the store without formal business involvement. She explains she always had hired help for washing and ironing, typically a widow.

title: Life satisfaction; marriage quality
description: Mabelle reflects that she wouldn't change anything in her life and describes her marriage as wonderful. She shows the interviewer a picture of her husband and discusses his reputation in the community.

title: Widowhood adjustment; social changes
description: Mabelle explains how working kept her from dwelling on grief. She discusses how her social circle changed when friends moved away to Spokane and Moscow, leaving few contemporaries in Elk River.

title: Current friendships; letter writing
description: Mabelle mentions her membership in a homemakers group that doesn't include her old friends. She describes maintaining friendships through letters with people in California, Spokane, and Canada.

title: Sister's estate; grandson's death
description: Mabelle discusses her 90-year-old sister in Moscow who can no longer live alone and the complications of settling her estate. She mentions the recent death of her grandson Bill in January.

title: Grandchildren; new baby
description: Mabelle explains she has two grandchildren, both through son John. She shares news that Bill's sister just gave birth to a boy, making Jandalee a cousin.

title: Release form; Bill's final days
description: The interview concludes with administrative matters and Mabelle sharing memories of Bill, his love for Elk River, his printing office work, and his desire to return to the community.
